# Bāverujātaka (Ja 339)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bāverujātaka* (Ja 339) is a narrative in the canonical Pali Jātaka collection. Set at Jetavana, the Buddha relates the story to illustrate how non-Buddhist teachers (*titthiyā*) lost their followers, gains, and renown after the appearance of the Buddha [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897]. In the story, sea merchants journey to the kingdom of Bāveru—a land previously devoid of birds—taking with them a common crow that is lavishly pampered and honored by the amazed locals [Cowell 1897]. On a subsequent voyage, the merchants bring a magnificent, trained peacock (the Bodhisatta); enchanted by the peacock's beauty and dance, the people revere the peacock instead, and the crow is relegated to a dunghill [Cowell 1897]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha explains that the crow was Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and the peacock was himself, comparing the eclipsing of the crow's fame to the eclipsing of sectarians once the Buddha proclaimed the Dhamma [Fausböll 1883; Cowell 1897].

 DharmaNexus registers Pali-internal text reuse between this Jātaka and the commentary, specifically the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Majjhimanikāye Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā* (§0.4–4.4 aligned with §1453_4–1461) [DharmaNexus].
